name: Blackwall railway electric telegraph
summary: From 1840 the London and Blackwall Railway used Cooke and Wheatstone electric telegraphs to send instructions to its winding-engine operators, an early working use of telegraphy on a railway.
description: Cooke and Wheatstone telegraph instruments on the London and Blackwall Railway, carrying instructions to winding-engine operators.
tier_reason: Prefer a bounded railway application tier; the current object/service is not the whole Cooke–Wheatstone telegraph invention. This is a scoped consequence judgement, not a reward for documentation or representation.
why: The line's carriages were hauled by rope from stationary winding engines, so engine operators needed instant word on when to start and stop.

date.basis: Evidence for this dated community entry; not necessarily the first possible use.

links.statement: The English needle-telegraph system used on the Blackwall railway embodied the current-induced magnetic-needle deflection observed in Oersted’s experiments.
links.scope: The scientific effect and railway signal instruments, with intervening development; no identity of the physical apparatus.
links.alternatives: Schilling, Muncke, Ampere, Wheatstone and others made distinct intervening contributions; other telegraph types need not use needles.
links.caveats: Cooke contested Hamel’s claim that a specific earlier Schilling apparatus had been copied into English service. The exact service date of the surviving five-needle specimen is not separately established.
links.timing: 1820 scientific observation precedes 1840 railway use; the surviving catalogue object may represent a later instrument.
